transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello. I suppose... well, what brings me in today is something that's been bothering me a fair bit lately. It's honestly a little embarrassing to admit. You see, since I stopped working, I spend a good chunk of my week down at the local museum. It’s a wonderful place, keeps me out of the house and gives me a sense of purpose, you know? Anyway, right now we're putting together all the plans for the next art walk. It's a big community event, takes a lot of coordinating, so naturally, there are always folks needing to discuss the details with me. 

But the problem is, people at the museum will come up and be talking right to me about the next art walk—standing right there in front of me—and I’ll be looking right at them, making eye contact, nodding along. But then... I don't know, I just suddenly realize I completely missed the middle of what they said. It's like a whole chunk of the conversation just vanished into thin air while I was staring right at their face. And then they stop talking, waiting for my input, and I have to swallow my pride, apologize, and ask them to run it by me again. It's just so frustrating, having people look at you like you don't care about what they're saying, when you really are trying to listen.
During these moments when you miss what they are saying, is your mind wandering off to other thoughts, or does everything just go completely blank?

Gosh, you know... I've asked myself that very same question. I really have. And honestly, I'm just not entirely sure. I've tried to catch myself in the act, so to speak, just to see what exactly is happening up there. 

Just last Tuesday, Mary—she handles the local watercolors for us, lovely lady, been volunteering at the museum since the late nineties—she was telling me about the easel placements for the main foyer. And I was looking right at her, right at her glasses. She has these thick red frames, and I remember noticing how perfectly they matched her scarf. But then... well, did my mind keep wandering off about the scarf? Or did it just shut off completely and go blank? I really couldn't tell you. 

It’s a bit like... well, it’s like when you fall asleep in a recliner in front of the television, and you don't realize you were asleep until you wake up with a jerk. You don't remember the exact moment you drifted off, and you don't necessarily remember dreaming about anything, you just know time passed and you missed the end of your program. So, I suppose I don't really know where my brain goes. It's just... away. And it takes me a good minute to even realize it's gone, which is the worst part, because by then Mary has finished her whole thought and is standing there waiting for me to say whether the easels should go by the north window or the coat check. It really makes me feel foolish, at my age, not even knowing what my own brain is doing while I'm standing right there on the museum floor. But to answer your question, I just don't know if it's wandering or blank. It's just a gap.
During the day, do you often find yourself feeling unusually drowsy or struggling to stay awake?

No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I brought up falling asleep in the recliner just as a sort of comparison, you know, to explain the feeling of losing time. But I'm not actually falling asleep during the day. I've always been a fairly energetic person, even now that I'm retired. I get up at a reasonable hour—usually around six-thirty, maybe seven if the cat doesn't wake me up demanding his breakfast. And once I'm up, I'm up. I make my coffee, read the paper, and then I'm off to the museum or running errands. 

I don't need naps, never really have. My brother, now, he's a different story. He can't get through an afternoon without dozing off in his chair, but I've always been the type who likes to keep moving. If I sit still for too long, I get a bit restless, actually. So, no, I'm not feeling drowsy or struggling to keep my eyes open when I'm talking to Mary or anyone else at the museum. I feel perfectly awake, perfectly alert. I've had my coffee, I'm standing on my own two feet, looking right at them. It's just my brain that seems to take a little vacation without telling me, not my body. It's not a tiredness thing at all, which almost makes it more baffling, if you think about it. If I were tired, well, that would make sense, wouldn't it? But I'm wide awake.

I remember, clear as day, being a boy in grade school. We lived over on Elm Street back then, a nice little house with a big oak tree in the front yard. Anyway, I remember my mother—God rest her soul—she used to keep all my old report cards in this big cedar chest at the foot of her bed. And I remember looking through them once when I was older, and almost every single one from when I was a little fellow, you know, before I was even twelve years old, they all had these notes from the teachers. Mrs. Gable in third grade, Mr. Henderson in fifth... they all wrote things like, "He daydreams too much," or "Needs constant reminders to finish his work." 

And it wasn't just at school, either. Oh, no. Homework was a whole ordeal in our house. My mother, she was a saint, she really was. She would have to pull up a chair from the kitchen table—one of those heavy wooden ones with the vinyl seats that stuck to your legs in the summer—and she would sit right there beside me. Just to keep me on track. If she got up to stir a pot on the stove or answer the telephone, my mind would just wander right off. I'd be staring out the window at the neighbor's dog, or fiddling with the eraser on my pencil until it broke off. She had to sit right there and tap the paper and say, "Focus now, let's get this math done." 

So, I suppose this whole business of my brain taking a vacation... it's not a new thing at all. It's just that now, instead of Mrs. Gable telling me to finish my spelling words, it's Mary waiting for me to tell her where to put the easels. But yes, to answer your question, it's been happening since I was just a boy.
